newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: VANSTONE SAYS JOBS OUTLOOK POSITIVE
Employment minister Amanda Vanstone says the outlook for later in the year is positive, even though employment figures for March are flat.
The jobless rate fell point-one-of-a per-cent to 8.7 per cent in March but there was a big fall in the number of Australians with jobs because fewer are looking for work.
Senator Vanstone says the most important thing is the continued steady growth in the trend figures.
She says the month-to-month drop in employment is to be regretted but the economic signs point to a very positive outlook for later in the year.
BORBIDGE WARNING TO HOWARD OVER NATIVE TITLE
Queensland's Premier Rob Borbidge says the Queensland National Party's support of John Howard could end if the Federal Government doesn't ensure security of tenure for pastoral lease holders.
Mr Borbidge has been pushing for the Federal Government to provide a legislative solution to confusion over Native Title, following the Wik decision.
He says his working relationship with John Howard will be over if he doesn't deliver on the issue.
Mr Borbidge says he has supported John Howard through thick and thin at substantial personal and political cost, and any working relationship has to be a two way street.
KERNOT SAYS WALLIS REPORT A MIXED BAG
Democrats Leader Cheryl Kernot has accused the Wallis Inquiry into Australia's financial system of "whimping out" on the issue of bank fees and charges.
Senator Kernot has criticised the report for not putting a ceiling on bank fees and charges, and says it basically means that banks can charge what they like.

But speaking at a National Consumers Federation conference in Melbourne, Senator Kernot praised the report for saying "on record" that large scale foreign bank ownership is not in Australia's national interest.
GOVERNMENT REVIEW OF DRUG REGULATION

The Federal Government says the crux of its review of drug regulation Australia, is achieving a balance between protecting public health and providing regulation that's not an undue burden on industry.

Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health, Chris Ellison, says the review into Therapeutic Goods Administration will produce a more efficient and streamlined approach to the regulation of medicinal products.

The changes include improved access to drugs that help sufferers of rare illnesses, improving the access to complimentary drugs including herbals, vitamins, minerals and nutritional therapies, and an overhaul of the export arrangements for medicinal products.
Senator Ellison says the review will give both consumers, and industry more confidence in Australian medicines.
KRAFT COULD FACE THOUSANDS OF CLAIMS OVER PEANUT BUTTER
A lawyer involved in a class action over contaminated peanut butter says the compensation bill may run into many millions of dollars.
An agreement has been reached on a process to resolve victims' claims against Kraft and General Foods.
The class action currently involves 700 victims.
Outside the Federal Court, solictor Peter Gordon, said anyone who consumed contaminated brands of peanut butter and became ill, was entitled to make a claim.
And he says thousands of people ate the brands of peanut butter involved.
COLLEGE OF GPs REJECTS AMA'S CLAIM
The Royal Australian College of GP's has released a survey of attitudes to euthanasia among GPs, that contradicts the AMA's claim that the majority are opposed to it.
The AMA's claim that 90 per cent of doctors oppose voluntary euthanasia, is based on a study done six months ago.
The College of GPs claims 56 per cent of members support assisted suicide in the final stage of a terminal illness.
Sixty-eight per cent believe euthanasia is an act of caring.
But the AMA's Vice President, Dr David Brand, says he's not convinced by the results.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
